chapters.title: Chapter 3: Constructing and Testing a Factor Strategy

lessons.title: Building a Factor Score: Ranking, Z-Scores, and Composite Signals

body.text: A factor score is not a formula you memorise once, it is a six-step assembly line: clean the data, standardise each metric, fix the direction, decide whether to neutralise sector bets, blend the metrics, and only then rank. Skip or botch any one step and the final score quietly measures the wrong thing.

children.text: Chapter 2 introduced the composite z-score idea briefly while covering the value factor. This lesson slows down and builds the entire pipeline properly, the same one used, in substance, by every NSE factor index and every serious quant desk, from raw, messy company data all the way to a ranked, tradeable list of stocks.
Step 1: Define the Universe and Handle Outliers

markDefs.definition: Capping extreme values in a dataset at a chosen threshold, such as the 1st and 99th percentile, before further analysis, so a handful of outliers do not distort a statistic like the mean or standard deviation.

children.text: Before any ranking happens, define which stocks are even eligible, typically NSE and BSE listed companies above a minimum market capitalisation and trading liquidity threshold, with a minimum listing history so newly listed companies with limited data do not distort the universe. Then deal with outliers. Financial ratios are notoriously fat-tailed: a company with near-zero earnings can show a P/E of 400, and a single such stock can drag a universe's average P/E far from where most stocks actually sit. The standard fix is
, capping every value at a chosen percentile, commonly the 1st and 99th, before any further calculation, rather than deleting the affected stocks outright.
A raw P/E of 8 and a raw dividend yield of 5% cannot be combined directly, they live on entirely different scales. Standardising converts every metric into a common, comparable unit.

body.caption: The z-score: how many standard deviations stock i's raw value sits from the universe mean, computed fresh at every rebalance date

columns.label: Z-Score
points: Preserves the magnitude of difference between stocks, not just their order
Sensitive to outliers and to how fat-tailed the underlying metric's distribution is
Requires winsorisation first to avoid one extreme value distorting the mean and standard deviation for everyone

columns.label: Percentile Rank
points: Converts each stock into its relative position in the ranked list, robust to outliers by construction
Loses information about how large the gap actually is between the 1st and 2nd ranked stock
Simpler and often preferred when a metric has a few extreme, hard-to-clean values

children.text: A higher composite score should always mean 'more attractive' before you combine metrics, and different raw metrics do not naturally agree on which direction that is. A high P/E is unattractive for value, but a high dividend yield is attractive. Before averaging, every metric where a low raw value is good, P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA, needs its z-score multiplied by minus one, or equivalently, you compute the z-score of its inverse, such as earnings yield instead of P/E. Forgetting this step is one of the most common, and most silent, bugs in a first attempt at factor construction, the code runs without error, it just ranks the most overpriced stocks as the most attractive ones.

Computing a z-score against the entire universe means a stock's score partly reflects which sector it happens to sit in. If metals stocks as a group are trading cheap because commodity prices are depressed, a whole-universe value z-score will flag most metals names as attractive, largely capturing a sector-level bet rather than genuine stock-specific mispricing within the sector. Sector-neutral scoring fixes this by computing each stock's z-score only against its own sector peers, isolating the pure, within-sector factor signal. The trade-off is real: sector-neutral construction deliberately gives up any return from correctly timing which sectors are cheap or expensive as a whole, in exchange for a cleaner, more targeted factor signal. Whether that trade-off is worth it depends on whether you believe sector-level cheapness itself carries useful information, or is mostly noise you would rather strip out.
Step 5: Combine Into a Composite Score

With every metric standardised and direction-corrected, combining them is usually a simple average of the z-scores, equal-weighting each metric. It is tempting to instead assign higher weights to whichever metric you believe is most predictive, but a large body of quant research has repeatedly found that simple equal-weighting tends to be at least as robust out of sample as more elaborate, optimised weighting schemes, which are prone to overfitting the specific historical period they were tuned on. Most published NSE factor index methodologies, and most professional quant desks, lean towards equal or simply-motivated weights for exactly this reason.
Worked Example: A Six-Stock Value Composite, Start to Finish

Six entirely hypothetical companies, Stock A through Stock F, none of them real NSE-listed names, illustrate the full pipeline using two metrics, P/E and dividend yield. The universe mean P/E is 14.67 with a standard deviation of 5.65; the universe mean dividend yield is 2.67% with a standard deviation of 1.52%. P/E is inverted before combining, since a lower P/E should score higher.

body.caption: Worked value composite, ranked from most to least attractive (hypothetical companies)

body.text: Stock A tops the ranking because it scores well on both metrics, a low P/E and a high dividend yield, not because of either one alone. Stock F sits close to zero, meaning it is roughly average on this composite, neither notably cheap nor notably expensive relative to this small universe. This is exactly what a composite score is meant to do: reward stocks that look attractive across multiple, independent lenses, rather than stocks that happen to win on a single metric.

children.text: Once every stock has a composite score, Chapter 1's construction choices come back into play: pick a breakpoint, commonly a quintile or decile, and decide how to weight the selected stocks. Two common options are equal weighting every stock that clears the breakpoint, which is simple and avoids concentration risk, or score-proportional weighting, tilting more capital towards the highest-scoring names, which increases the strategy's exposure to the factor but also its concentration in a smaller number of names. In the worked example above, an equal-weighted top-two portfolio would split capital evenly between Stock A and Stock E, while a score-proportional version would tilt meaningfully more towards Stock A given its notably higher composite score.
The same six steps translate directly into a short pandas pipeline. This is illustrative structure, not a complete, production-ready script.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("nse_universe.csv")  # symbol, sector, pe_ratio, dividend_yield

# Step 1: winsorise extreme values at the 1st and 99th percentile
for col in ["pe_ratio", "dividend_yield"]:
    lower, upper = df[col].quantile([0.01, 0.99])
    df[col] = df[col].clip(lower, upper)


def zscore(s):
    return (s - s.mean()) / s.std()


# Step 2 and 4: standardise within each sector (sector-neutral)
df["z_dividend_yield"] = df.groupby("sector")["dividend_yield"].transform(zscore)

# Step 3: invert P/E direction so a lower P/E scores higher
df["z_pe_inverted"] = df.groupby("sector")["pe_ratio"].transform(zscore) * -1

# Step 5: equal-weighted composite of the two standardised metrics
df["value_score"] = df[["z_pe_inverted", "z_dividend_yield"]].mean(axis=1)

# Step 6: rank and select the top quintile
df["rank"] = df["value_score"].rank(ascending=False)
top_quintile = df[df["rank"] <= len(df) * 0.2]
body.caption: The six-step factor score pipeline as a short pandas script

body.title: Compute a Z-Score
body.prompt: Using the same universe as the worked example (mean P/E = 14.67, standard deviation = 5.65), a seventh hypothetical stock, Stock G, has a P/E of 20. What is Stock G's raw P/E z-score (before any direction flip), rounded to two decimal places?
body.explanation: z = (20 - 14.67) / 5.65 = 5.33 / 5.65 ≈ 0.94. Since this is the raw z-score before flipping direction, a positive value here means Stock G has an above-average, less attractive P/E; after inverting for direction in Step 3, its value z-score for P/E would be approximately -0.94.

body.title: Test Yourself: Why Winsorise?
body.question: Why is winsorising extreme values typically done before computing z-scores, rather than after?
options: It makes the code run faster
An extreme outlier can distort the universe's mean and standard deviation, which would then distort every other stock's z-score, not just the outlier's own
It is a purely cosmetic step with no effect on the resulting scores
Z-scores cannot be computed at all if any outliers are present
body.explanation: Because the mean and standard deviation used in the z-score formula are calculated across the whole universe, a single extreme outlier can pull the mean and inflate the standard deviation, which distorts the z-score of every other stock in the universe, not just the outlier itself. Winsorising first prevents this contamination.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: Capping extreme values at a chosen percentile threshold before analysis, so outliers do not distort the mean and standard deviation used to compute z-scores.
Flipping the sign of a metric's z-score (or scoring its inverse) so that a higher composite score always means 'more attractive', consistent across all metrics being combined.
Computing a stock's z-score relative only to its own sector peers rather than the whole universe, isolating the within-sector factor signal at the cost of giving up any sector-level timing bet.
Weighting selected stocks in proportion to their composite factor score, tilting more capital towards higher-conviction names at the cost of greater concentration.

body.text: The worked example in this lesson uses entirely hypothetical companies and numbers for teaching purposes only, and the code sample is illustrative structure, not a complete or production-ready script. This is not investment advice or a recommendation regarding any real security.

points: Building a factor score is a six-step pipeline: define the universe and handle outliers, standardise each metric, correct direction, decide on sector neutrality, combine into a composite, then convert the score into portfolio weights
Winsorisation caps extreme values before scoring, since a single outlier can distort the mean and standard deviation used for every stock's z-score
Z-scores preserve magnitude but are outlier-sensitive; percentile ranks are outlier-robust but lose magnitude information
Forgetting to flip direction on metrics like P/E, where lower is better, is a common, silent bug that ranks unattractive stocks as attractive
Sector-neutral scoring isolates the pure, within-sector factor signal but gives up any return from sector-level timing
Equal-weighting standardised metrics into a composite tends to be at least as robust out of sample as more complex, optimised weighting schemes
